doc01_search_engines:
Search engines help people locate useful information in a very large collection of web pages. Their work normally begins before a user types anything. A crawler discovers pages, a parser extracts readable text, and an indexing component records the terms found in each page. The result is a searchable representation of the web rather than a slow scan of every page at query time.

When a user submits a query, the query processor normalizes the words and looks them up in the index. It creates a set of matching documents and may apply Boolean operators, phrase rules, or spelling suggestions. A ranking module then decides which of the matches should be shown first. Good ranking balances textual relevance, document quality, and sometimes signals from links or user behaviour.

The interface is also important. Users need a clear search box, understandable result titles, and short document previews. This WebMiningSearch project models the central ideas with a small local corpus. Although the collection is tiny compared with a public search engine, it demonstrates the same information-retrieval pipeline: collect, preprocess, index, search, rank, and display results.
doc02_inverted_index:
An inverted index maps each term to the documents containing that term. For example, the term network may point to document two and document seven. This structure makes search fast because the system can jump directly from a query term to its posting list instead of reading every document again.

A posting list usually contains sorted document identifiers. If a query contains two terms, the search system can intersect the two sorted lists for an AND query or combine them for an OR query. Document frequency records how many documents contain a term. Term frequency records how often the term occurs inside one particular document. These counts are later useful for TF-IDF ranking.

The index is called inverted because it reverses the ordinary document-to-words relationship. A normal document stores many words, but an inverted index stores each word followed by the documents in which it occurs. The project builds this data structure from fifteen text files. It also builds a positional index, which adds word locations for phrase and proximity retrieval.
doc03_web_crawling:
A web crawler discovers pages by following hyperlinks. It begins with one or more seed addresses, downloads their pages, extracts outgoing links, and places unseen links in a queue. Crawling policies control which pages are visited, how often they are revisited, and how duplicate pages are avoided. A real crawler must also respect robots rules and avoid sending too many requests to the same website.

The crawler cannot normally visit every page on the web. It chooses a schedule based on importance, freshness, topic relevance, and available resources. News pages may require frequent revisits, while an old reference page may change only rarely. Duplicate detection is useful because copied content wastes storage and can produce repetitive search results.

After collection, crawled pages are cleaned and passed to the indexer. Navigation menus, advertisements, and scripts are less useful than the main article text. In this local assignment the corpus already consists of prepared text documents, so a full crawler is not required. The document still explains the collection stage that would precede indexing in a web-scale system.
doc04_page_ranking:
Page ranking estimates the importance or relevance of a web page. Link analysis can treat a link as a recommendation, while content ranking compares query terms with document terms. A document containing the query repeatedly may be relevant, but repetition alone is not enough because a page can artificially repeat words without providing useful information.

Link-based methods such as PageRank distribute importance through hyperlinks. A page linked by many respected pages may receive a stronger importance signal than a page with no incoming links. Content-based methods use term frequency, inverse document frequency, headings, titles, and field weights. Modern systems combine many signals rather than trusting a single formula.

This project uses TF-IDF and cosine similarity for content ranking. TF gives credit when a query term occurs in a document. IDF gives more credit to a distinctive term than to a very common one. Cosine similarity compares the weighted query vector with each weighted document vector, producing a score used to order the results.
doc05_text_preprocessing:
Text preprocessing prepares raw text for indexing and search. The same concept may appear as Search, search, or search followed by punctuation. Lowercasing and punctuation cleanup make these forms consistent. Tokenization then splits a document into individual words or tokens that the index can store and compare.

Stop words are very frequent grammatical words such as the, and, and is. They can be removed from ordinary word retrieval because they often do not distinguish one document from another. However, a positional index should keep normalized word positions so that an exact phrase can still be checked correctly. This project therefore separates cleaned indexing tokens from the full normalized token sequence used for positions.

Stemming is another common preprocessing technique. A stemmer may reduce computing, computed, and computation to a shared root. The tradeoff is that an aggressive stemmer can merge words that have different meanings. The current project keeps the implementation transparent by using lowercasing, tokenization, and a small stop-word list before introducing more advanced retrieval features.
doc06_tf_idf:
TF-IDF gives high weight to terms that occur often in one document but rarely across the collection. A common term receives a lower inverse document frequency than a distinctive term. For example, a word appearing in nearly every document provides little evidence that one result is especially relevant, while a rare technical word can strongly distinguish a focused document.

Term frequency counts a word within one document. Raw frequency can overvalue a word repeated many times, so retrieval systems often use a logarithmic TF weight. Document frequency counts how many documents contain the word. Inverse document frequency is calculated from the collection size and document frequency. The product of TF and IDF becomes the word's weight in the document vector.

The query is represented as a vector using the same vocabulary. Cosine similarity divides the dot product of the query and document vectors by their lengths. This normalization prevents long documents from winning merely because they contain more words. The ranked-search mode in the graphical interface prints cosine scores in descending order.
doc07_boolean_queries:
Boolean retrieval supports AND, OR, and NOT operators. A search for crawler AND index returns documents containing both words. A query with NOT removes unwanted documents. This model treats each document as either a match or a non-match; it does not initially decide which match is more important.

AND is implemented by taking the intersection of two posting lists. OR is implemented by taking their union. NOT is implemented by subtracting one posting list from the full collection or from another matching set. For instance, search AND NOT mining keeps documents mentioning search while excluding documents that also mention mining.

Boolean expressions are useful when a user has a precise information need. A researcher can require one concept and exclude another concept that creates noise. The first Boolean module in this project accepts one binary operation at a time, such as search AND retrieval or crawler OR ranking. The result is displayed as a list of matching document identifiers and previews.
doc08_phrase_search:
Phrase search uses word positions. The phrase information retrieval matches only when information is immediately followed by retrieval in the same document. An ordinary inverted index can tell that two words occur in a document, but it cannot prove that they appear together in the requested order.

A positional index solves this problem by storing a list of locations for every term in every document. If information occurs at position seven and retrieval occurs at position eight, that pair is a phrase match. For a longer phrase, each following term must occur at the next position. The search engine first finds documents containing all phrase terms and then checks their position lists.

Phrase retrieval is more precise than a simple AND query. A document that contains information at the start and retrieval much later should match information AND retrieval but should not match the exact phrase. Users commonly place quotation marks around a phrase in public search engines. In the local GUI, selecting Phrase mode applies the same adjacent-position rule to the entered words.
doc09_proximity_search:
Proximity search finds terms that occur near each other without requiring an exact phrase. Data NEAR three mining can match data mining methods when the two words are separated by at most three positions. It is useful when authors express the same idea with small variations, extra adjectives, or connecting words.

The positional index stores every normalized word location. A proximity algorithm compares locations for the left term with locations for the right term. In this project, the notation data /3 mining means that mining must follow data with zero, one, two, or three words between them. The order therefore remains meaningful, unlike an unordered near operator.

Proximity retrieval offers a middle ground between Boolean AND and exact phrase matching. AND can return a document where the terms are far apart, while phrase search can miss a relevant sentence containing a descriptive word. The graphical interface validates the simple word / number word format and shows all documents satisfying the requested maximum gap.
doc10_wildcard_queries:
Wildcard search matches a pattern against the vocabulary rather than requiring an exact word. A prefix pattern can retrieve computer, computing, and computation without requiring the user to know the exact word form. The asterisk represents any sequence of letters, so a pattern can be placed at the end or in the middle of a word.

The retrieval system first identifies every vocabulary term matching the wildcard expression. It then takes the union of their posting lists to find documents containing any expanded term. In this small collection, scanning the vocabulary is easy to understand and fast enough. A large search engine would often use a permuterm index, k-gram index, or another specialized structure to make wildcard expansion efficient.

Wildcard queries improve recall, but very broad patterns can match many vocabulary terms and produce a large result set. Users should therefore choose a meaningful prefix whenever possible. The GUI's Wildcard mode displays both the expanded vocabulary terms and the documents they match, making the expansion process visible for learning and demonstration.
doc11_spelling_correction:
Spelling correction suggests a close vocabulary word for a misspelled query. Levenshtein distance measures the number of character insertions, deletions, or substitutions needed to change one word into another. A common one-letter omission in retrieval is only one deletion away from the intended term.

The search engine compares the unknown word with its known vocabulary. Candidates with a lower edit distance are usually better suggestions. Several candidates can have the same distance, so another signal is useful for tie breaking. Character n-grams provide such a signal by representing a word through short overlapping letter sequences. Similar spellings tend to share more n-grams.

The tolerant-retrieval module returns a short ordered suggestion list. It does not silently rewrite the user's query; instead it exposes the possible corrections so that the user can choose. This behaviour is safer for a learning project and makes the relationship between misspelling, vocabulary, edit distance, and n-gram similarity easy to explain.
doc12_ngrams:
Character n-grams break a word into short overlapping sequences. They help a retrieval system compare similar spellings and generate candidates for query correction. A bigram representation of a word includes pairs of neighbouring letters, often with boundary markers at the beginning and end.

For example, two similar spellings share many of their bigrams even when one letter is missing or substituted. The system can compare the n-gram sets using Jaccard similarity: the number of shared n-grams divided by the number of n-grams in either set. A higher score suggests that two strings are structurally similar.

N-grams are also useful for wildcard retrieval and approximate matching. A search engine may use them to limit a huge vocabulary to a smaller set of likely candidates before calculating edit distance. In this project the n-gram function is used as a transparent secondary comparison for spelling suggestions, following the more direct Levenshtein-distance ordering.
doc13_soundex:
Soundex encodes words according to an approximate English pronunciation. A tolerant search engine can use Soundex to find names that sound alike even when their spelling differs. The code preserves the first letter and converts later consonants into numeric groups, producing a short code such as S620.

Words with the same Soundex code are not guaranteed to have the same meaning. Instead, Soundex offers a simple phonetic candidate filter. It is especially useful for names, where spelling differences and pronunciation variations are common. The search module can calculate the code for a user word and then list vocabulary terms with the same code.

In this collection, the misspelled query sarch shares a Soundex code with search. This demonstrates a tolerant technique different from edit distance: the character sequence is not compared directly, but similar pronunciation is approximated. Soundex is not perfect for every language or accent, yet it remains a useful and easy-to-demonstrate retrieval feature.
doc14_synonyms:
Synonym expansion can improve recall. A query for automobile may also search for car, while a query for information retrieval may include search and document retrieval. Users often choose different words for the same concept, so an exact vocabulary match can miss documents that are relevant but expressed differently.

The synonym dictionary in this project is intentionally small and explicit. It maps automobile to car, car to automobile, engine to search, and web to internet. The entered term remains in the expanded query, and its related terms are added. The system then combines postings lists for all available expansion terms.

Synonym expansion must be used carefully. Some words have several meanings, and adding every possible related word can reduce precision. A controlled dictionary is appropriate for a focused corpus because it makes the chosen relationships visible. The GUI shows the expansion terms before listing the matching documents, so users can understand why additional results appear.
doc15_web_mining:
Web mining discovers useful patterns from web content, links, and user behaviour. Content mining analyzes page text, structure mining analyzes links, and usage mining analyzes activity logs. These three areas apply data-mining ideas to the unusual scale, connectivity, and variety of the web.

Web content mining extracts knowledge from documents, images, metadata, and other page material. Web structure mining studies links between pages, often using graph algorithms to identify authorities and hubs. Web usage mining examines logs and interaction trails to understand navigation, recommendations, and common user paths.

Information retrieval and web mining are related but distinct. Retrieval focuses on finding documents that answer a user's current query. Mining focuses on discovering broader patterns that may support analysis, personalization, or decision making. A search engine can use mining results to improve ranking and recommendations, while a mining system can use an inverted index to locate relevant textual evidence efficiently.
doc16_association_rules:
Association rule mining discovers patterns of items that occur together. A classic market basket rule has the form bread AND butter implies milk. Support measures how frequently an item set occurs, while confidence measures how often the consequence appears when the condition is present.

The Apriori algorithm searches for frequent item sets level by level. It uses the principle that an infrequent subset cannot produce a frequent larger set. Association rules are useful in recommendation systems, retail analysis, and website navigation analysis. A web store can recommend related products after observing common combinations in previous transactions.

Rules should be evaluated carefully because a high confidence value can be misleading when the consequence is already very common. Lift compares the observed co-occurrence with the expected independent occurrence. Data mining therefore combines support, confidence, lift, and domain knowledge before treating a discovered association as useful.
doc17_clustering:
Clustering groups similar data items without requiring labelled training examples. The goal is to discover natural structure in a collection. A document collection can be clustered by the words it contains, while customers can be clustered by their behaviour or preferences.

K-means is a popular clustering method. It chooses a number of centers, assigns each item to its nearest center, and repeatedly updates the centers. Hierarchical clustering instead builds a tree of groups. The quality of a clustering result depends on the feature representation, distance function, and number of requested groups.

Web mining can use clustering to organize search results into topics. Instead of presenting a long flat list, a system may group results about networks, databases, security, or machine learning. Clusters can improve exploration, but their labels need to be understandable so that users can choose the topic that matches their information need.
doc18_neural_networks:
Neural networks are machine-learning models inspired by layers of connected processing units. Each connection has a numeric weight, and each layer transforms its inputs into a new representation. During training, the model adjusts weights to reduce the difference between predictions and known answers.

Deep learning refers to neural networks with many hidden layers. Convolutional networks are effective for images, while transformer architectures are widely used for language tasks. Training requires data, a loss function, an optimization method, and careful evaluation on examples not used during learning.

Information retrieval can use neural models for semantic ranking, query understanding, and document representation. A traditional TF-IDF engine is easier to inspect and explain, while a neural ranker can learn more complex relationships. Practical systems often combine lexical retrieval for reliable candidate generation with learned ranking for final ordering.
doc19_computer_networks:
Computer networks connect devices so that they can exchange data using shared protocols. The Internet protocol suite organizes communication into layers. Applications use services such as web browsing and email, while lower layers deliver packets across local networks and wide-area links.

IP addressing identifies hosts and routers. TCP provides reliable ordered delivery through acknowledgements and retransmission, while UDP provides lightweight datagrams when speed is more important than reliability. Routers choose paths between networks and switches forward frames inside a local network.

Search engines depend on networks to crawl pages and serve results. A crawler downloads documents through network requests, and a user receives ranked results from remote servers. Network latency, bandwidth, caching, and failure handling all influence the speed and reliability of a web search experience.
doc20_databases:
Database systems store structured information and provide efficient ways to create, read, update, and delete records. A relational database organizes data into tables connected by keys. SQL queries select rows, combine tables, filter conditions, and calculate summaries.

Indexes are important in both databases and search engines. A database index maps key values to record locations, while an inverted index maps terms to document identifiers. Both structures trade storage and update work for faster queries. Transaction systems also provide consistency and recovery when many users access data concurrently.

NoSQL databases use models such as key-value stores, documents, graphs, and wide columns. They can support flexible schemas and distributed workloads. A web-mining application may store crawled pages, link graphs, click logs, and generated indexes in different database systems depending on the access pattern and scale.
doc21_cloud_computing:
Cloud computing delivers computing resources over a network. Instead of buying and operating every server, an organization can use virtual machines, managed databases, object storage, and serverless functions when required. Resources can scale up during busy periods and scale down afterward.

Infrastructure as a Service provides virtual infrastructure, Platform as a Service provides deployment environments, and Software as a Service provides complete applications. Virtualization and containers isolate workloads while allowing many services to share physical hardware. Monitoring and automation help operators detect failures and manage changing demand.

A large search engine commonly runs on distributed cloud-like infrastructure. Crawling, indexing, query serving, log analysis, and machine-learning training can be separate services. The local WebMiningSearch application runs on one computer, but its modular design mirrors the separation of responsibilities used in larger systems.
doc22_cybersecurity:
Cybersecurity protects systems, networks, applications, and information from unauthorized access or harmful changes. Common goals are confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Security controls include authentication, authorization, encryption, backups, monitoring, and incident response procedures.

Web applications face threats such as phishing, password attacks, malware, cross-site scripting, injection, and denial of service. Secure software validates input, stores passwords safely, applies least privilege, and keeps dependencies updated. Network security uses firewalls, segmentation, and encrypted connections to reduce exposure.

Search systems must protect crawlers, stored documents, and user queries. Malicious pages can attempt to exploit parsers or manipulate ranking through spam links and repeated keywords. Logging, rate limits, safe content handling, and privacy-aware retention policies help maintain a trustworthy retrieval service.
doc23_cryptography:
Cryptography protects information by transforming it with mathematical algorithms and secret keys. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for encryption and decryption. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key, allowing secure key exchange and digital signatures.

Hash functions create fixed-size fingerprints of data. A secure hash makes it difficult to recover the original message or find two messages with the same fingerprint. Digital signatures combine private-key operations and hashes to prove authenticity and detect changes to a document.

Web security uses protocols such as TLS to protect communication between a browser and a server. Retrieval systems may encrypt data in transit, protect stored index files, and authenticate administrative actions. Cryptography supports privacy and trust, but it must be combined with correct key management and secure application design.
doc24_robotics_vision:
Robotics combines sensors, computation, and actuators so that machines can perceive and act in the physical world. A robot may use cameras, lidar, microphones, and position sensors to observe its environment. Planning algorithms choose actions that help the robot reach a goal safely.

Computer vision extracts information from images and video. Tasks include object detection, image classification, tracking, and scene understanding. Modern vision systems often use neural networks trained on large labelled datasets, while classical methods use features, edges, geometry, and statistical models.

Web-scale image and video search relies on retrieval ideas similar to text search. Content can be represented by visual descriptors, captions, metadata, and learned embeddings. An index helps locate likely candidates quickly, after which a ranking model orders the most relevant images or videos for the user's query.
doc25_big_data:
Big data describes collections that are too large, fast, or varied for simple processing on one machine. The common characteristics are volume, velocity, variety, and sometimes veracity and value. Distributed storage and parallel computation help organizations process data from transactions, sensors, logs, and web applications.

MapReduce is a programming model that divides a task into map operations and reduce operations. The map stage produces intermediate key-value pairs, and the reduce stage combines values for the same key. Distributed systems must also manage failures, data locality, replication, and uneven work distribution.

Web mining produces big data through crawled pages, link graphs, search queries, and interaction logs. Index construction can be divided across machines, while query servers can replicate indexes to answer requests quickly. The small corpus in this assignment demonstrates the same ideas at a scale where every structure can be inspected directly.
